name: OMK 2A Heme — Summative 3 Objective Review · Board-Style Set 2

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy who emigrated from Greece 1 year ago is brought to the office by his parents for evaluation of chronic anemia. He has received transfusions only intermittently. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows frontal bossing, prominence of both maxillae with dental malocclusion, and conjunctival pallor. The liver is palpated 3 cm and the spleen 6 cm below the costal margins. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 7.2 g/dL, a hematocrit of 22%, and a mean corpuscular volume of 61 μm3. An x-ray of the skull shows widening of the diploic space with perpendicular trabeculations. Which of the following best explains this patient's craniofacial and abdominal findings?
choices: A. Deposition of iron within the reticuloendothelial system from repeated transfusion
B. Expansion of hematopoietic tissue into sites normally inactive after infancy
C. Failure of the yolk sac to transition to hepatic hematopoiesis
D. Metastatic calcification of the facial skeleton from a raised calcium-phosphate product
E. Osteoblast activation by parathyroid hormone-related protein
questions.explanation: Hematopoiesis migrates over a lifetime: the yolk sac in the embryo → the fetal liver and spleen mid-gestation → bone marrow before birth → and in the adult it retreats out of the long bones into the AXIAL skeleton (vertebrae, ribs, sternum, pelvis), which is why a marrow biopsy is taken from the iliac crest and not the femur. Under extreme, sustained demand the body reopens the sites it abandoned. In beta-thalassemia major the marrow is driven relentlessly by ineffective erythropoiesis, so two things happen at once: EXTRAMEDULLARY hematopoiesis restarts in the liver and spleen → hepatosplenomegaly, and the existing marrow cavities of the skull and face expand → frontal bossing, maxillary prominence, and the widened diploic space with perpendicular trabeculations described on the skull film. The findings are a marrow trying to keep up, not a storage or metabolic process.

wrongExplanations.0: Iron deposition is a genuine and serious problem in a chronically transfused thalassemic, and would be the answer for bronze skin, cardiomyopathy, cirrhosis, or diabetes. It does not enlarge the marrow cavity or expand the facial bones, and this boy has been transfused only intermittently.
wrongExplanations.2: The yolk-sac-to-liver transition is a normal embryonic event completed long before birth. A failure of it would be incompatible with survival to age 7, and it does not describe reactivation of a site later in life.
wrongExplanations.3: Metastatic calcification requires a raised calcium-phosphate product, as in chronic kidney disease or hyperparathyroidism, and deposits in soft tissues such as vessels, kidney, and lung rather than expanding the diploic space.
wrongExplanations.4: Parathyroid hormone-related protein drives osteoCLAST-mediated bone resorption and hypercalcemia as a paraneoplastic syndrome, most classically in squamous cell carcinoma. It would produce lytic destruction and a high calcium, not symmetric marrow expansion in a child with a microcytic anemia.

questions.eli5: Before birth, blood is made in the yolk sac, then the liver, then finally the bones. His bone marrow is working so hard to keep up that it swells the skull and cheekbones outward, and his liver and spleen have switched blood-making back on. The changed face shape is the body making room for more marrow.

questions.stem:
A 62-year-old woman with a 9-year history of rheumatoid arthritis comes to the office because of fatigue for 4 months. Her medications are methotrexate and folic acid. She has had no melena or hematochezia, and menses ceased 11 years ago. Her temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 78/min, and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. Physical examination shows symmetric swelling of the metacarpophalangeal joints of both hands with ulnar deviation. There is no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. A test of the stool for occult blood is negative. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                          10.1 g/dL
    Hematocrit                          31%
    Mean corpuscular volume             84 μm3
    Red cell distribution width         13.0% (N=11.5–14.5)
    Reticulocyte count                  0.8%
    Serum iron                          28 μg/dL
    Total iron-binding capacity         210 μg/dL
    Serum ferritin                      340 ng/mL
    Serum creatinine                    0.9 mg/dL
    Erythrocyte sedimentation rate      62 mm/h

Which of the following best explains this patient's low serum iron concentration?
choices: A. Blunted release of erythropoietin from the kidney in response to cytokines
B. Direct cytokine-mediated suppression of erythroid precursors in the marrow
C. Hepcidin-mediated blockade of iron export from macrophages and enterocytes
D. Impaired intestinal iron absorption caused by methotrexate
E. Occult gastrointestinal blood loss depleting total body iron stores
questions.explanation: This is anemia of inflammation — the most common anemia among hospitalized patients in the United States, and the one most often mistaken for iron deficiency and treated with iron that does nothing. The iron studies separate them decisively: iron deficiency gives a HIGH iron-binding capacity, a LOW ferritin, and a HIGH red cell distribution width; anemia of inflammation gives a LOW binding capacity, a HIGH ferritin (an acute-phase reactant), and a NORMAL width. Serum iron is low in both and discriminates nothing. Interleukin-6 drives hepatic hepcidin synthesis, and hepcidin degrades ferroportin — the only exit iron has from a macrophage or an enterocyte. Lock that door and serum iron falls while total body iron stays normal or high. Read it as a doorman locking the exits: the iron is in the building, it just cannot reach the marrow.

wrongExplanations.0: Blunted erythropoietin release is a real mechanism in anemia of inflammation and contributes to the anemia — but it acts on the marrow's drive to produce, not on iron handling. It would not lower the serum iron concentration, which is what this question asks about.
wrongExplanations.1: Direct cytokine suppression of erythroid precursors is likewise a genuine mechanism here, and it explains the low reticulocyte count. It operates independently of iron and would leave the serum iron untouched.
wrongExplanations.3: Methotrexate causes megaloblastic changes through folate antagonism, which is why she takes folic acid alongside it. It does not impair iron absorption, and it would raise rather than lower the mean corpuscular volume.
wrongExplanations.4: Occult blood loss would be the answer with a LOW ferritin and a HIGH iron-binding capacity — true iron deficiency. Her ferritin of 340 ng/mL and binding capacity of 210 μg/dL are the opposite pattern, and the stool test is negative.

questions.eli5: Her joints are inflamed all the time, and inflammation makes a hormone that locks iron inside storage cells. Her body has plenty of iron — it just cannot get it out to build red blood cells. That is why the blood test shows low iron but very high stored iron, and why iron pills would not help.

questions.stem:
A 68-year-old woman with stage 4 chronic kidney disease has been receiving epoetin alfa for anemia. Two weeks ago her hemoglobin concentration was 9.4 g/dL and her blood pressure was 132/78 mm Hg. She feels well today and has no chest pain, dyspnea, or leg swelling. Her ferritin concentration is 280 ng/mL and her transferrin saturation is 32%. Her temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 74/min, and blood pressure is 158/94 mm Hg. Laboratory studies today show:

    Hemoglobin              11.8 g/dL
    Hematocrit              36%
    Platelet count          224,000/mm3

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: A. Continue the current dose and repeat the hemoglobin measurement in 4 weeks
B. Discontinue epoetin alfa and transfuse one unit of packed red blood cells
C. Increase the epoetin alfa dose to target a hemoglobin concentration of 13 g/dL
D. Reduce the epoetin alfa dose
E. Substitute intravenous iron for epoetin alfa
questions.explanation: Two numbers govern every erythropoiesis-stimulating agent, and this patient has crossed both. ELEVEN IS THE CEILING: every boxed warning turns on a hemoglobin above 11 g/dL, where there is increased death, myocardial infarction, stroke, venous thromboembolism, and vascular access thrombosis with NO additional benefit. And ONE IN TWO: a rise of more than 1 g/dL in any 2-week period mandates a dose reduction — hers rose 2.4 g/dL. Her new hypertension reinforces it, since hypertension is the most common adverse effect, occurring in up to a third of treated patients. Think of the drug as a thermostat set to 'just warm enough to avoid transfusion,' never to 'comfortable.' Every boxed warning ends in the same sentence: use the lowest dose needed to avoid transfusion.

wrongExplanations.0: Continuing unchanged would be the answer if the hemoglobin were still below 11 g/dL and rising by less than 1 g/dL per 2 weeks. Both rules have been breached here, and waiting another 4 weeks allows the level to climb further into the range where harm is documented.
wrongExplanations.1: Transfusion would be the answer for symptomatic anemia at a hemoglobin below 7 g/dL. Her hemoglobin is 11.8 g/dL and she is asymptomatic — transfusing would be exactly backwards.
wrongExplanations.2: Targeting 13 g/dL is the trap: it treats a laboratory value as though normal were the goal. Every trial that pushed the hemoglobin toward normal showed more cardiovascular events and deaths without benefit, which is the reason the ceiling exists.
wrongExplanations.4: Iron matters enormously with these agents, since driving the marrow consumes iron fast — but she is iron replete (ferritin 280 ng/mL, saturation 32%). Iron is given ALONGSIDE the agent when stores are low, not as a substitute for adjusting an overshooting dose.

questions.eli5: The drug tells her bone marrow to build red blood cells, and it worked too well and too fast. Pushing the count higher does not make people feel better — it causes strokes, heart attacks, and clots. Her blood pressure went up too, so the dose comes down.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother because of fever and lethargy for 6 hours. He underwent splenectomy 3 years ago after traumatic splenic rupture in a bicycle collision. His mother is unsure whether his vaccinations are current. His temperature is 39.8°C (103.6°F), pulse is 148/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure is 78/40 mm Hg. He is difficult to rouse. Physical examination shows mottled skin, purpuric lesions over both legs with dusky centers, and a capillary refill time of 4 seconds. There is no meningismus. A peripheral blood smear shows erythrocytes containing small, round, densely staining nuclear remnants. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: A. Administration of empiric intravenous antibiotics
B. Administration of intravenous immune globulin
C. Obtaining blood cultures and observing pending the results
D. Performing a lumbar puncture before initiating antibiotic therapy
E. Vaccination against Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae type b
questions.explanation: The Howell-Jolly bodies on the smear confirm what the history says — he has no functioning spleen. The spleen is the body's principal filter for ENCAPSULATED organisms, and without it opsonized bacteria are not cleared, so a bloodstream infection can progress to overwhelming sepsis within HOURS rather than days. Streptococcus pneumoniae dominates the risk, followed by Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae type b. He already has purpura fulminans and shock. The single intervention that saves lives in overwhelming post-splenectomy sepsis is immediate empiric antibiotics without waiting for anything, which is exactly what asplenic patients and their families are taught: any fever is an emergency. The three-part prevention strategy — vaccinate (before the splenectomy when it is planned), daily penicillin prophylaxis in children, and educate the family — matters enormously, but it belongs to the outpatient visit, not to this one.

wrongExplanations.1: Intravenous immune globulin has a role in specific antibody deficiencies such as Bruton agammaglobulinemia. It is not a treatment for acute bacterial sepsis and would do nothing in the hours that decide this child's outcome.
wrongExplanations.2: Drawing cultures is correct and should happen — but OBSERVING pending results is the error that kills these patients. The window here is measured in hours, and cultures take a day or more.
wrongExplanations.3: A lumbar puncture may be appropriate later, and he has no meningismus. Delaying antibiotics for any procedure is the specific mistake this scenario is built to test; when the two conflict, antibiotics go first.
wrongExplanations.4: Vaccination is the cornerstone of PREVENTION and should have been given before or shortly after the splenectomy — it is what was likely missed here. Administering a vaccine to a child already in septic shock provides no protection against the organism currently killing him.

questions.eli5: The spleen is a filter that catches a particular family of bacteria, and his was removed after an accident. Without it, an infection can go from fine to life-threatening in a few hours. Antibiotics have to go in right now — everything else, including tests, waits.

questions.stem:
A 32-year-old woman has ongoing bleeding after an emergency cesarean delivery performed for placental abruption. She has received 6 units of packed red blood cells and 4 units of plasma over the past 2 hours. She continues to ooze from the surgical incision and from every intravenous puncture site. Her temperature is 36.4°C (97.5°F), pulse is 124/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 92/58 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                                  9.1 g/dL
    Platelet count                              96,000/mm3
    Prothrombin time                            17 sec (N=11–14)
    Activated partial thromboplastin time       42 sec (N=25–35)
    Fibrinogen                                  68 mg/dL (N=200–400)
    D-dimer                                     Markedly increased

Which of the following is the most appropriate product to administer next?
choices: A. Albumin
B. Cryoprecipitate
C. Factor VIII concentrate
D. Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate
E. Platelets
questions.explanation: Obstetric hemorrhage with abruption has produced disseminated intravascular coagulation — prolonged clotting times, a consumed fibrinogen, and a high D-dimer. Match the product to the specific deficit rather than to the diagnosis. The outlier here is the fibrinogen at 68 mg/dL, and cryoprecipitate is the cold-insoluble fraction of thawed plasma, concentrated in fibrinogen. The reason plasma cannot fix this is a volume problem, not a content problem: plasma carries fibrinogen only at PHYSIOLOGIC concentration, so replacing a severe deficit would require a volume the patient cannot receive — the ocean and the teacup. She has already had 4 units of plasma and her fibrinogen is still 68 mg/dL, which makes the point for her.

wrongExplanations.0: Albumin is a colloid volume expander and contains NO coagulation factors at all. It would raise her blood pressure briefly while doing nothing for a patient who is bleeding because she cannot form fibrin.
wrongExplanations.2: Factor VIII concentrate is the specific product for hemophilia A — an ISOLATED factor VIII deficiency. This patient has a multifactor consumptive coagulopathy, and her limiting deficit is fibrinogen.
wrongExplanations.3: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate is the answer for urgent WARFARIN reversal with serious bleeding, given with vitamin K. She is not taking warfarin, and the concentrate contains no fibrinogen.
wrongExplanations.4: Platelets would be the answer for a count below about 50,000/mm3 in a surgically bleeding patient, or below 10,000/mm3 in a stable hypoproliferative one. At 96,000/mm3 her platelet count is adequate for hemostasis and is not what is limiting her clot.

questions.eli5: Fibrinogen is the protein that forms the actual mesh of a clot, and hers has been used up. Plain plasma has fibrinogen in it, but only at normal strength — she would drown before getting enough. Cryoprecipitate is the concentrated version, so a small bag delivers what she needs.

questions.stem:
A 28-year-old woman comes to the office because of easy bruising and bleeding from her gums when she brushes her teeth for 2 weeks. She had an upper respiratory tract illness 3 weeks ago that resolved without treatment. She takes no medications and does not drink alcoholic beverages. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows petechiae over both shins and scattered petechiae on the buccal mucosa. There is no lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                                  13.2 g/dL
    Leukocyte count                             6,800/mm3, normal differential
    Platelet count                              9,000/mm3
    Prothrombin time                            12 sec (N=11–14)
    Activated partial thromboplastin time       31 sec (N=25–35)

A peripheral blood smear shows markedly reduced platelets with occasional large forms; erythrocytes and leukocytes appear normal and no fragmented cells are seen. Bone marrow examination shows normal to increased numbers of megakaryocytes. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
choices: A. Corticosteroid therapy
B. Plasma exchange
C. Platelet transfusion
D. Romiplostim
E. Splenectomy
questions.explanation: Isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal hemoglobin, normal leukocytes, normal clotting times, and no schistocytes — often following a viral illness — is immune thrombocytopenic purpura. The buried clue is the marrow: megakaryocytes are normal to INCREASED, which proves production is intact and the platelets are being destroyed in the periphery by autoantibody. That single fact dictates the treatment. Because the mechanism is immune destruction, therapy is directed at the immune process: corticosteroids first line, with intravenous immune globulin when a faster rise is needed. The large platelets on the smear are young platelets the marrow is pushing out to compensate.

wrongExplanations.1: Plasma exchange is the treatment for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, which requires a microangiopathic hemolytic anemia — schistocytes, a falling hemoglobin, a high lactate dehydrogenase. Her hemoglobin is 13.2 g/dL and her smear shows no fragmented cells.
wrongExplanations.2: Platelet transfusion is the trap. The 10,000/mm3 transfusion threshold applies specifically to HYPOPROLIFERATIVE thrombocytopenia, where the marrow cannot make platelets. Here the destruction is peripheral, so transfused platelets are destroyed just as fast as her own — transfusion is reserved for serious active bleeding.
wrongExplanations.3: Romiplostim is a thrombopoietin receptor agonist and does work in this disease, but it is a second-line agent for patients who fail or cannot tolerate corticosteroids. It also pushes a marrow that is already producing normally.
wrongExplanations.4: Splenectomy removes the principal site of antibody-coated platelet destruction and is effective, but it is reserved for disease refractory to medical therapy. Operating on a treatment-naive patient with a platelet count of 9,000/mm3 would be premature and dangerous.

questions.eli5: Her immune system is tagging her own platelets for destruction, but her bone marrow is building them normally — the marrow test proves it. Pouring in donated platelets just gives the antibodies more targets. The fix is to calm the immune system down with steroids.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man is evaluated after a second unprovoked deep venous thrombosis of the leg. His mother, a maternal aunt, and his maternal grandfather each had venous thromboembolism before the age of 45 years. He takes no medications and does not smoke cigarettes. During his first episode 2 years ago, intravenous unfractionated heparin failed to prolong the activated partial thromboplastin time despite escalating doses and confirmed administration. Physical examination shows no abnormalities other than mild swelling of the left calf. Laboratory studies show a normal platelet count, a prothrombin time of 12 seconds (N=11–14), and an activated partial thromboplastin time of 29 seconds (N=25–35). Which of the following is the most likely underlying abnormality?
choices: A. Antithrombin deficiency
B. Elevated factor VIII activity
C. Factor V Leiden mutation
D. Protein C deficiency
E. Prothrombin G20210A mutation
questions.explanation: Heparin has no intrinsic anticoagulant activity — it works entirely by binding ANTITHROMBIN and accelerating its inhibition of thrombin and factor Xa by about a thousandfold. If antithrombin is deficient, there is little for heparin to potentiate, so the activated partial thromboplastin time will not budge no matter how much is given. That failure is the buried clue and it names the deficiency. It also places him in the dangerous half of the thrombophilias: LOSING A BRAKE beats pushing the accelerator. Antithrombin, protein C, and protein S deficiencies are rare but carry a relative risk of 15–19×, whereas factor V Leiden and prothrombin G20210A are common and carry only 3–5×. His strong autosomal dominant family history of early thrombosis and a second unprovoked event at 22 fit the high-risk group.

wrongExplanations.1: Elevated factor VIII activity is an acquired prothrombotic state and a genuine risk factor, but it is not inherited in this pattern and does not interfere with heparin. Heparin would work normally.
wrongExplanations.2: Factor V Leiden is the surface-read answer — it is the most common thrombophilia, present in about 5% of Caucasians and accounting for 20–30% of venous thromboembolism. But its relative risk is only 3–5×, and crucially it does not blunt heparin: the defect is resistance of factor V to activated protein C, not a failure of the heparin-antithrombin axis.
wrongExplanations.3: Protein C deficiency belongs to the same high-risk 'lost brake' group and fits the family history, but it does not impair heparin. Its signature complication is warfarin-induced skin necrosis, because protein C falls fastest when warfarin is started.
wrongExplanations.4: Prothrombin G20210A is a mutation in the 3-prime untranslated region that stabilizes the messenger RNA, so more prothrombin is made. The protein itself is entirely normal, heparin works normally, and the relative risk is only 3–5×.

questions.eli5: Heparin does not thin blood by itself — it supercharges a natural brake protein the body already has. He barely has that protein, so heparin had nothing to work with and the test never changed. Missing a brake is far more dangerous than having a mildly overactive accelerator.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman comes to the office because of swelling and aching of the left leg for 3 days. She returned 5 days ago from a 10-hour intercontinental flight. She has no history of cancer and takes no medications. Her temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 86/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows the left calf to be 4 cm greater in circumference than the right, with pitting edema to the mid-shin and tenderness along the course of the deep venous system. There is no erythema, warmth, or ulceration. The skin of the second toe of the left foot can be tented easily between the examiner's fingers at the interdigital web space. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
choices: A. Compression (duplex) ultrasonography of the left leg
B. Contrast venography of the left leg
C. Lymphoscintigraphy
D. Measurement of the serum D-dimer concentration
E. Ventilation-perfusion scanning
questions.explanation: Duplex ultrasonography is the standard imaging test for suspected deep venous thrombosis, and it is the first move in ANY unilateral swollen limb — for a blunt reason: a deep venous thrombosis can kill, and the alternatives on the differential cannot. Her pretest probability is high (a recent 10-hour flight, unilateral swelling, 4 cm of calf asymmetry, tenderness along the deep system), which is exactly when imaging comes first. Note the deliberate negative: the web space TENTS easily, so the Stemmer sign is absent. A positive Stemmer sign — skin that cannot be tented, giving the squared-off toes of lymphedema — is the pathognomonic bedside finding that points away from thrombosis. Its absence here removes the main competing diagnosis and leaves the dangerous one.

wrongExplanations.1: Contrast venography is the historical gold standard but is invasive, requires contrast, and has been replaced by ultrasonography for first-line diagnosis. It would be considered only if the ultrasound were nondiagnostic and suspicion remained high.
wrongExplanations.2: Lymphoscintigraphy images lymphatic drainage and would be the answer for suspected lymphedema — which requires a POSITIVE Stemmer sign, and typically a history of nodal dissection, radiation, or filariasis. Her web space tents easily, and imaging the lymphatics first would delay exclusion of a lethal diagnosis.
wrongExplanations.3: D-dimer is the near-miss. It is useful to EXCLUDE thrombosis in a patient with LOW pretest probability, because its value lies in its negative predictive value. In a high-probability patient a negative result does not exclude the diagnosis and a positive result adds nothing, so it cannot substitute for imaging here. (Separately, a persistently elevated D-dimer after anticoagulation is stopped predicts recurrence.)
wrongExplanations.4: Ventilation-perfusion scanning is the screening test of choice for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, not for a swollen leg. She has no dyspnea, hypoxemia, or tachycardia to suggest pulmonary embolism.

questions.eli5: A swollen leg on one side after a long flight is a blood clot until proven otherwise, and an ultrasound answers that in minutes. The examiner also checked whether the skin between her toes could be pinched up — it could, which argues against a lymph-drainage problem. Clots can kill, so you rule that out first.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 8 weeks' gestation comes to the office because of pain and swelling of the left leg for 2 days. Compression ultrasonography shows a nonocclusive thrombus in the left femoral vein. This is her first thrombotic event. She has no history of bleeding, her platelet count is normal, and her creatinine clearance is normal. Anticoagulation is to be started. Which of the following is the most appropriate agent?
choices: A. Apixaban
B. Dabigatran
C. Enoxaparin
D. Rivaroxaban
E. Warfarin
questions.explanation: Enoxaparin is a low-molecular-weight heparin, and the choice is decided by what crosses the placenta. Heparins — both unfractionated and low molecular weight — are large, highly charged molecules that do NOT cross, which makes them the anticoagulants of pregnancy; low-molecular-weight heparin is also the agent used while breastfeeding. Warfarin is small, crosses freely, and is a recognized teratogen: exposure in the first trimester causes the warfarin embryopathy of nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses, and later exposure causes central nervous system abnormalities and fetal bleeding. Pregnancy and breastfeeding are the first entry on the list of situations where a direct oral anticoagulant must NOT be used — they are not established as safe and do reach the fetal circulation and breast milk. The other carve-outs on that list are worth carrying alongside it: massive clot burden where thrombolysis may be needed, extremes of body weight, altered gastrointestinal anatomy, and antiphospholipid syndrome, where there is evidence of actual harm.

wrongExplanations.0: Apixaban is otherwise attractive — it is one of the two direct oral anticoagulants that can be started orally from the first dose without a heparin lead-in, and it is the preferred agent in renal impairment and may have the lowest bleeding risk of the four. None of that applies in pregnancy, where it is contraindicated.
wrongExplanations.1: Dabigatran is contraindicated in pregnancy for the same reason. It also is not a monotherapy agent: like edoxaban, it requires 5–10 days of initial low-molecular-weight heparin before switching.
wrongExplanations.3: Rivaroxaban shares apixaban's oral loading advantage and shares the pregnancy contraindication. Fixed oral dosing also cannot be titrated or stopped quickly, which matters if delivery or bleeding intervenes.
wrongExplanations.4: Warfarin is the actively dangerous option here. It crosses the placenta and is teratogenic, with a well-described embryopathy from first-trimester exposure — precisely the window this patient is in.

questions.eli5: Some blood thinners are small enough to cross into the baby and cause birth defects. Heparin molecules are too big and charged to cross, so they stay in the mother's bloodstream where they are needed. That is why it is the standard choice in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man underwent percutaneous coronary intervention with placement of a drug-eluting stent 6 weeks ago and has been taking aspirin 81 mg daily and clopidogrel 75 mg daily since. Four weeks ago he was started on omeprazole for reflux symptoms. He now comes to the emergency department because of crushing substernal chest pain for 1 hour. He reports taking every dose of both antiplatelet drugs. An ECG shows ST-segment elevation in the anterior leads, and coronary angiography shows thrombotic occlusion within the previously placed stent. Which of the following best explains the failure of his antiplatelet therapy?
choices: A. Aspirin 81 mg daily is an inadequate maintenance dose after stent placement
B. Clopidogrel irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase-1, an effect antagonized by omeprazole
C. Omeprazole displaces clopidogrel from plasma protein binding sites
D. Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, preventing conversion of clopidogrel to its active metabolite
E. Omeprazole raises gastric pH, reducing absorption of clopidogrel
questions.explanation: Clopidogrel is a PRODRUG. It has no antiplatelet activity as swallowed and must be oxidized by hepatic CYP2C19 into the active metabolite that irreversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 adenosine diphosphate receptor. Omeprazole is a CYP2C19 inhibitor, so it blunts that conversion and leaves the patient effectively on aspirin alone with a fresh stent in place. Two practical consequences follow: use PANTOPRAZOLE if a proton pump inhibitor is needed, since it does not meaningfully inhibit CYP2C19, and remember that genetic poor metabolizers get little benefit from clopidogrel for the same reason. Ticagrelor sidesteps the problem entirely because it is not a prodrug — though it brings its own testable features, namely dyspnea, bradyarrhythmias, and a requirement that maintenance aspirin stay at or below 100 mg daily.

wrongExplanations.0: 81 mg daily is the correct maintenance dose of aspirin after stenting; higher maintenance doses increase bleeding without improving outcomes. (The reverse rule applies to ticagrelor, where aspirin must be kept at or below 100 mg or the ticagrelor loses effect.)
wrongExplanations.1: This confuses the two drugs. Aspirin irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase-1; clopidogrel irreversibly blocks the P2Y12 receptor. Omeprazole does not antagonize cyclooxygenase at all.
wrongExplanations.2: Protein-binding displacement is a generically plausible-sounding mechanism that does not apply here. Clopidogrel's problem with omeprazole is a failure of hepatic ACTIVATION, not competition for albumin.
wrongExplanations.4: Raising gastric pH is a real and important interaction — for oral IRON, which requires the ferrous form and an acidic duodenum to be absorbed. Clopidogrel absorption is not pH-dependent; the interaction is metabolic, not absorptive.

questions.eli5: Clopidogrel arrives in the body switched off, and a liver enzyme has to switch it on. His heartburn medicine blocks that exact enzyme, so the pills he faithfully swallowed never became the active drug. Swapping to a different heartburn medicine avoids the clash.

questions.stem:
A 74-year-old man comes to the office because of a 6-month history of progressive fatigue. He received chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma 8 years ago and has been in remission since. He takes no medications and has had no bleeding, fever, or weight loss. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 84/min, and blood pressure is 138/82 mm Hg. Physical examination shows conjunctival pallor. There is no lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                  8.6 g/dL
    Hematocrit                  26%
    Mean corpuscular volume     104 μm3
    Leukocyte count             2,900/mm3
      Segmented neutrophils     28%
    Platelet count              78,000/mm3
    Reticulocyte count          0.5%
    Serum vitamin B12           480 pg/mL (N=200–900)
    Serum folate                Within normal limits

A peripheral blood smear shows oval macrocytes, neutrophils with only two nuclear lobes and sparse granules, and occasional large platelets; blasts are 3% of leukocytes. Bone marrow biopsy shows a HYPERCELLULAR marrow with dysplastic changes in all three lineages and 6% blasts. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: A. Acute myeloid leukemia
B. Aplastic anemia
C. Megaloblastic anemia due to vitamin B12 deficiency
D. Myelodysplastic syndrome
E. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
F. Primary myelofibrosis
questions.explanation: The defining paradox of myelodysplastic syndrome is on display: the marrow is HYPERCELLULAR yet the patient is pancytopenic. Production is not reduced — it is WASTED, because the cells being built are structurally abnormal and die before or shortly after leaving the marrow. On the map of hematologic malignancy it occupies the middle box: not undifferentiated like acute leukemia, not normally differentiated like the myeloproliferative neoplasms, but ABNORMALLY differentiated. The hypolobated, hypogranular neutrophils described here are that dysplasia made visible. His prior chemotherapy is the buried clue, since alkylating agents cause therapy-related disease years later. The pathophysiology is epigenetic, which is exactly why hypomethylating agents (azacitidine, decitabine) are the disease-directed treatment; allogeneic transplant is the only cure. About 30% progress to acute myeloid leukemia, and 50% die of the cytopenias themselves.

wrongExplanations.0: Acute myeloid leukemia requires 20% or more blasts in marrow or blood. He has 6% in the marrow and 3% in the blood. That single line is what separates myelodysplastic syndrome from acute leukemia — and it is the same line that separates accelerated from blast phase chronic myeloid leukemia.
wrongExplanations.1: Aplastic anemia produces pancytopenia from a HYPOcellular marrow — mostly fat with few hematopoietic cells. His marrow is hypercellular, which is the opposite finding and excludes it directly.
wrongExplanations.2: B12 deficiency also causes macrocytosis, pancytopenia, and a low reticulocyte count, and is the closest nutritional mimic. It is excluded by the normal B12 and folate levels, and its neutrophils are HYPERsegmented with five or more lobes, whereas his are hypolobated with only two.
wrongExplanations.4: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria can cause pancytopenia, but it is a hemolytic disease — it would show intravascular hemolysis with hemoglobinuria, a high lactate dehydrogenase, and absent CD55 and CD59 on flow cytometry, along with thrombosis at unusual sites.
wrongExplanations.5: Primary myelofibrosis would show a leukoerythroblastic smear — teardrop-shaped erythrocytes with nucleated red cells and immature granulocytes — together with massive splenomegaly and a fibrotic, often inaspirable marrow. He has no organomegaly and no teardrop cells.

questions.eli5: His bone marrow is packed full of cells, yet his blood counts are all low. The factory is running at full speed but building defective products that fall apart before they ship. That mismatch — a crowded marrow with an empty bloodstream — is the signature of this disease.

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old man comes to the office because of a 6-month history of headache, dizziness, and intense generalized itching that begins within minutes of taking a hot shower. He also describes episodic burning pain with redness and warmth of both hands and feet. He does not smoke cigarettes and has no history of lung disease or sleep apnea. He takes no medications and uses no diuretics. His temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 76/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 152/94 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. Physical examination shows facial plethora and conjunctival injection; the spleen is palpated 4 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                  19.8 g/dL
    Hematocrit                  59%
    Leukocyte count             13,400/mm3
    Platelet count              588,000/mm3
    Serum erythropoietin        2 mU/mL (N=4–24)

Which of the following is the most likely underlying abnormality?
choices: A. A gain-of-function mutation in JAK2
B. A mutation in the von Hippel-Lindau gene
C. Chronic hypoxemia due to obstructive sleep apnea
D. Ectopic erythropoietin production by a renal cell carcinoma
E. Reduced plasma volume due to diuretic use
questions.explanation: The erythropoietin level is the item. When the marrow is being DRIVEN from outside — hypoxia, a tumor, exogenous administration — erythropoietin is HIGH. When the marrow is producing autonomously, the normal feedback loop suppresses erythropoietin, so it is LOW. A low erythropoietin with a high hematocrit means a primary marrow disease: polycythemia vera, driven by a gain-of-function JAK2 mutation that leaves the JAK2/STAT pathway signalling continuously. Three further features confirm it. All three lineages are up (panmyelosis), not just red cells. There is splenomegaly. And the symptoms are the characteristic ones: aquagenic pruritus (itching after a hot shower) and erythromelalgia. Because the cells produced are mature and functional, the danger in this family of diseases is THROMBOSIS, not marrow failure — which is also why JAK2 testing belongs in the workup of an unexplained splanchnic vein thrombosis.

wrongExplanations.1: Von Hippel-Lindau mutations impair degradation of hypoxia-inducible factor, so the kidney behaves as though it were hypoxic and makes MORE erythropoietin. The level would be high or inappropriately normal, not suppressed to 2 mU/mL.
wrongExplanations.2: Chronic hypoxemia from sleep apnea is a genuine cause of secondary polycythemia, but it drives erythropoietin UP. His oxygen saturation is 98%, he has no sleep apnea history, and his erythropoietin is suppressed.
wrongExplanations.3: An erythropoietin-secreting renal cell carcinoma raises the hormone by definition. It also would not explain the leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, aquagenic pruritus, or splenomegaly, all of which point to a marrow that is expanding every lineage.
wrongExplanations.4: Diuretic-induced contraction gives RELATIVE polycythemia: the red cell mass is normal and only the plasma volume has fallen. It produces no splenomegaly, no pruritus, no erythromelalgia, and no rise in leukocytes or platelets — and he takes no diuretics.

questions.eli5: The kidney normally sends a hormone telling the marrow to make red cells, and it stops sending it when there are already enough. His hormone level is nearly zero, yet his marrow keeps building anyway — it has stopped listening. A permanently jammed 'on' switch in a signalling protein is the cause.

questions.stem:
A 24-year-old man comes to the office because of painless swelling on the left side of his neck for 2 months. He also reports generalized itching and says the swollen area begins to ache within minutes of drinking beer. He has had drenching night sweats and a 5-kg (11-lb) weight loss. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. His temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), pulse is 82/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a 4-cm firm, rubbery, nontender left supraclavicular node and several matted left cervical nodes. The spleen is palpated 2 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                              11.9 g/dL
    Leukocyte count                         9,800/mm3
      Eosinophils                           8%
    Platelet count                          268,000/mm3
    Erythrocyte sedimentation rate          68 mm/h
    Lactate dehydrogenase                   310 U/L

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
choices: A. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy
B. Excisional lymph node biopsy
C. Fine-needle aspiration of the cervical node
D. Flow cytometry of peripheral blood
E. Serum protein electrophoresis
questions.explanation: Everything here says malignant rather than reactive lymphadenopathy: the nodes are firm, rubbery, nontender, matted, and larger than 2 cm; the location is SUPRACLAVICULAR, a red flag at any size; the course is progressive over months rather than regressing after a trigger; there are B symptoms; and the sedimentation rate and lactate dehydrogenase are raised. The specific combination of pruritus, ALCOHOL-INDUCED NODAL PAIN, and peripheral eosinophilia in a patient in the first peak of the bimodal age distribution (15–35 and over 55) is highly characteristic of Hodgkin lymphoma — alcohol intolerance is rare but essentially specific to it. The diagnosis depends on seeing the nodal ARCHITECTURE surrounding the rare Reed-Sternberg cells, so an intact node must be removed whole. Stage afterward with PET/CT and a sedimentation rate; treatment is ABVD and the disease is curable.

wrongExplanations.0: Marrow biopsy has a role in STAGING once the diagnosis is established, not in making it. Sampling the marrow of a patient whose disease is currently confined to nodes would most likely be normal and would not identify the tumor.
wrongExplanations.2: Fine-needle aspiration is the near-miss and the classic error. It retrieves a suspension of cells without architecture, and because Reed-Sternberg cells are RARE within a mostly reactive inflammatory infiltrate, the aspirate may sample only reactive cells and miss the diagnosis entirely.
wrongExplanations.3: Flow cytometry of blood is the right test when malignant cells are circulating, as in chronic lymphocytic leukemia or a leukemic lymphoma. His leukocyte count and differential are essentially normal, so there is nothing abnormal in the blood to phenotype.
wrongExplanations.4: Serum protein electrophoresis looks for a monoclonal paraprotein in myeloma or Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Those present with bone pain, renal failure, and hypercalcemia, or with hyperviscosity — not with itching, alcohol-induced nodal pain, and eosinophilia in a 24-year-old.

questions.eli5: The cancer cells in this disease are rare and scattered inside the lymph node, and the diagnosis depends on how the whole node is arranged around them. Poking it with a needle usually pulls out only the ordinary cells sitting nearby. The entire node has to come out intact.

questions.stem:
A 71-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his daughter because of blurred vision, vertigo, and unsteadiness of gait for 1 week. He has had fatigue and numbness of both feet for 6 months. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 142/86 mm Hg. Physical examination shows generalized lymphadenopathy and a spleen palpated 5 cm below the left costal margin. Funduscopic examination shows dilated, tortuous retinal veins with sausage-like segmentation. Sensation to vibration is decreased over both feet. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                  9.2 g/dL
    Hematocrit                  28%
    Serum total protein         9.8 g/dL
    Serum calcium               9.4 mg/dL
    Serum creatinine            1.0 mg/dL

Serum protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal IgM spike of 4.2 g/dL. A skeletal survey shows no lytic lesions. A peripheral blood smear shows erythrocytes stacked in linear aggregates resembling coins. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
choices: A. Bisphosphonate therapy
B. Emergent plasmapheresis
C. Hemodialysis
D. High-dose corticosteroid therapy
E. Radiation therapy to the involved lymph nodes
questions.explanation: An IgM paraprotein with blurred vision, vertigo, ataxia, and segmented retinal veins is hyperviscosity syndrome from lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (Waldenström macroglobulinemia). IgM is PENTAMERIC — a single enormous molecule — and that structure drives every complication: at high concentration it thickens plasma directly, so the retinal veins dilate and sludge and the brain is underperfused. Untreated it progresses to stroke, coma, and death, so the immediate treatment is emergent plasmapheresis to physically remove the protein; chemotherapy for the underlying clone follows, with attention to the IgM flare that can transiently worsen things at the start. The rouleaux on the smear are the same phenomenon seen on glass. Note what separates this from myeloma: myeloma attacks the SKELETON and the KIDNEY (hypercalcemia, renal failure, lytic lesions, usually IgG or IgA), while this patient has normal calcium, normal creatinine, no lytic lesions, prominent lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly, a peripheral neuropathy, and an IgM protein.

wrongExplanations.0: Bisphosphonates treat the skeletal complications of MYELOMA — lytic lesions and hypercalcemia. His skeletal survey is clean and his calcium is 9.4 mg/dL, and a bisphosphonate would do nothing for viscosity.
wrongExplanations.2: Hemodialysis would be the answer for the renal failure of light chain cast nephropathy, a myeloma complication. His creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL, and dialysis does not efficiently clear a large pentameric protein from plasma.
wrongExplanations.3: Corticosteroids are part of treating the underlying lymphoproliferative disease and reduce tumor burden over days to weeks. They do not lower plasma viscosity quickly enough for a patient who is already losing vision and balance.
wrongExplanations.4: Radiation to nodes treats localized bulk. It has no effect on the circulating IgM that is causing the emergency, and this is a diffuse, systemic disease.

questions.eli5: His blood is full of a giant antibody that makes it thick like syrup, so it cannot flow properly through the smallest vessels in his eyes and brain. That is why the retinal veins look like linked sausages. A machine has to filter the protein out of his plasma right away.

questions.stem:
A 66-year-old woman is found to have a serum total protein concentration of 8.9 g/dL on laboratory studies obtained during a routine health maintenance examination. She feels entirely well. She has had no bone pain, fractures, fatigue, or recurrent infections. She takes no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities; there is no bone tenderness, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                  13.4 g/dL
    Serum calcium               9.5 mg/dL
    Serum creatinine            0.8 mg/dL

Serum protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal IgG spike of 1.8 g/dL. Bone marrow biopsy shows 6% clonal plasma cells. A skeletal survey shows no lytic lesions. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: A. Autologous stem cell transplantation after induction therapy
B. Bortezomib, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone
C. Lenalidomide monotherapy as used in high-risk smoldering myeloma
D. Observation with repeat laboratory studies in 6 months
E. Radiation therapy to symptomatic bone lesions
questions.explanation: Two numbers separate the plasma cell states: 10 and 3. Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance is under 10% marrow plasma cells AND under 3 g/dL of monoclonal protein. Smoldering myeloma is 10–60% plasma cells OR 3 g/dL or more. She is below both thresholds — 6% and 1.8 g/dL — so this is a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance. What converts either precursor state into treated myeloma is END ORGAN DAMAGE, the CRAB tetrad: hyperCalcemia, Renal failure, Anemia, and Bone lesions. She has none — calcium 9.5 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, and a clean skeletal survey. NEITHER precursor state is treated; both are watched. Surveillance is electrophoresis, serum free light chains, a complete blood count and a metabolic panel every 6 months, with a skeletal survey at least annually. Her progression risk is about 1% per year and it is flat, so most patients with this finding never develop myeloma — but the 1% per year never stops, which is why the counselling pairs genuine reassurance with a real commitment to follow-up.

wrongExplanations.0: Autologous stem cell transplantation is a treatment for active myeloma in a fit patient. Applying it to a precursor state with no end organ damage would expose her to substantial toxicity to treat a condition that will most likely never progress.
wrongExplanations.1: Triplet therapy with a proteasome inhibitor, an immunomodulatory drug, and a corticosteroid is standard treatment for ACTIVE myeloma — that is, once CRAB features appear. None are present.
wrongExplanations.2: Lenalidomide monotherapy has been studied in high-risk SMOLDERING myeloma, which requires 10% or more plasma cells or a spike of 3 g/dL or more. She meets neither threshold, so even that indication does not apply.
wrongExplanations.4: Radiation therapy is used palliatively for a painful lytic lesion, a pathologic fracture, or cord compression from a plasmacytoma. She has no bone lesions and no symptoms to palliate.

questions.eli5: She has a small amount of one abnormal antibody in her blood, but nothing in her body has been harmed by it — her calcium, kidneys, blood count, and bones are all fine. Below certain cutoffs this is a finding to watch, not a cancer to treat. Most people with it never go on to develop myeloma.

questions.stem:
A 16-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of shortness of breath and facial swelling for 3 days. The swelling is worse when he lies flat. He has no history of serious illness. His temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows edema of the face and both upper extremities with distended neck veins and prominent superficial veins over the anterior chest wall. There is bilateral cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin              9.8 g/dL
    Leukocyte count         68,000/mm3
    Platelet count          62,000/mm3

A chest x-ray shows a large anterior mediastinal mass. Flow cytometry of peripheral blood shows a blast population expressing terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT), CD2, CD3, and CD7; CD19, CD10, CD33, and myeloperoxidase are not expressed. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: A. Acute myeloid leukemia
B. Burkitt lymphoma
C. Hodgkin lymphoma
D. Precursor B-cell lymphoblastic leukemia
E. Precursor T-cell lymphoblastic leukemia
F. Thymoma
questions.explanation: Read the immunophenotype in two steps. TdT is a marker of PRECURSOR (lymphoblastic) cells, so this is a lymphoblastic neoplasm rather than a mature lymphoid one. Then read lineage: CD2, CD3, and CD7 are T-cell markers, while CD19 and CD10 (B-cell) and CD33 and myeloperoxidase (myeloid) are absent. That gives precursor T-cell lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma, and the clinical picture is its signature — an adolescent male with a bulky ANTERIOR MEDIASTINAL mass arising in the thymus, compressing the superior vena cava to produce facial and upper limb edema with distended neck and chest wall veins. Prognostically this matters: favorable features in childhood leukemia are age 1–10 years, a leukocyte count below 50,000/mm3, hyperdiploidy, and t(12;21), while unfavorable features are age under 1 or over 10, a count above 50,000/mm3, t(9;22), central nervous system involvement, and a T-cell phenotype. He has three of the unfavorable ones.

wrongExplanations.0: Acute myeloid leukemia would express CD33, CD13, and myeloperoxidase, and its blasts may contain Auer rods. Both myeloid markers are explicitly absent here, and TdT would not be the dominant finding.
wrongExplanations.1: Burkitt lymphoma is a MATURE B-cell neoplasm — it is TdT NEGATIVE and expresses surface immunoglobulin with CD19 and CD20, carries t(8;14) driving MYC, and shows a starry-sky pattern on biopsy. It typically presents with an abdominal or jaw mass rather than a mediastinal one.
wrongExplanations.2: Hodgkin lymphoma can produce a mediastinal mass in this age group, but the malignant Reed-Sternberg cells express CD15 and CD30, are rare within a reactive infiltrate, and do not circulate as 68,000 blasts. There would be no blast population to phenotype.
wrongExplanations.3: Precursor B-cell disease is the near-miss and is the more common childhood leukemia overall. It is flipped by the lineage markers: it expresses CD19 and CD10 (the common acute lymphoblastic leukemia antigen) rather than CD2, CD3, and CD7, and it carries a better prognosis and rarely presents with a mediastinal mass.
wrongExplanations.5: A thymoma occupies the same anatomic compartment and can cause superior vena cava obstruction, but it is an epithelial tumor of adults, associated with myasthenia gravis and red cell aplasia. It does not produce circulating TdT-positive blasts or these blood counts.

questions.eli5: A marker called TdT says these are very immature cells, and the other markers say they are T cells. T-cell leukemia in a teenage boy classically grows as a mass in the middle of the chest, where the thymus sits. That mass is squeezing the big vein returning blood from his head and arms, which is why his face is swollen.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with metastatic melanoma has been receiving pembrolizumab for 10 weeks. He comes to the office because of eight watery stools daily for 5 days with lower abdominal cramping. He has had no fever, no recent travel, no antibiotic exposure, and no sick contacts. His temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Physical examination shows diffuse abdominal tenderness without guarding or rebound. Stool studies are negative for Clostridioides difficile toxin, ova and parasites, and enteric bacterial pathogens. Colonoscopy shows diffuse mucosal erythema with friability and shallow ulcerations extending from the rectum to the splenic flexure. Biopsy specimens show a dense lymphocytic infiltrate of the lamina propria with crypt abscesses and apoptotic bodies. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
choices: A. High-dose corticosteroid therapy
B. Loperamide for symptomatic control of the diarrhea
C. Metronidazole for presumed anaerobic infection
D. Octreotide for presumed secretory diarrhea
E. Oral vancomycin for Clostridioides difficile colitis
questions.explanation: Predict the toxicity from the CLASS. Cytotoxic chemotherapy injures fast-dividing tissue; targeted agents injure wherever the target is normally expressed (HER2 on cardiomyocytes, hence trastuzumab cardiotoxicity); hormonal agents cause hormone-withdrawal effects; and IMMUNOTHERAPY causes autoimmunity in any organ — the immune-related adverse events, which characteristically end in '-itis.' Pembrolizumab blocks PD-1, a checkpoint whose normal job is to limit autoimmunity by dampening T cells in peripheral tissues. Remove that brake and self-reactive T cells attack normal organs; colitis is among the most common and most dangerous, because untreated it progresses to perforation. The infectious workup is negative and the histology shows a lymphocytic infiltrate, so the treatment is immunosuppression — high-dose corticosteroids, escalating to infliximab or vedolizumab if steroid-refractory. The same logic explains checkpoint-inhibitor thyroiditis, hypophysitis, hepatitis, pneumonitis, and nephritis.

wrongExplanations.1: Loperamide would be reasonable for uncomplicated chemotherapy-associated diarrhea. Here it merely masks the symptom while immune-mediated inflammation continues, and slowing the bowel in an ulcerated colitis risks toxic megacolon and perforation.
wrongExplanations.2: Metronidazole treats anaerobic and parasitic infection and was once used for Clostridioides difficile. The stool studies are explicitly negative and the biopsy shows an immune infiltrate, not infection.
wrongExplanations.3: Octreotide is used for secretory diarrhea from neuroendocrine tumors such as carcinoid, and sometimes for refractory chemotherapy-induced diarrhea. It does not address an immune-mediated colitis and would not heal the ulceration.
wrongExplanations.4: Oral vancomycin is first-line for Clostridioides difficile colitis, which was specifically excluded by a negative toxin assay. Treating an absent infection would delay the immunosuppression this patient needs.

questions.eli5: His cancer drug works by taking the brakes off his immune system so it will attack the tumor. The trouble is those brakes also stopped it from attacking his own organs, and now it is attacking his colon. The treatment is to put a brake back on with steroids.

questions.stem:
A 72-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department from a nursing facility because of confusion for 6 hours. Staff report she is normally alert and fully oriented. She has a history of recurrent urinary tract infections. Her temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), pulse is 116/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg. She is oriented to person only. Auscultation of the chest shows clear lung fields. There is suprapubic tenderness. Urinalysis shows numerous leukocytes and bacteria. Laboratory studies show:

    Leukocyte count         18,400/mm3
    Platelet count          122,000/mm3
    Serum creatinine        1.9 mg/dL (baseline 0.9)
    Serum lactate           3.4 mmol/L (N=0.5–2.2)

Which of the following is this patient's quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA) score?
questions.explanation: qSOFA has exactly three components, each worth one point: RESPIRATORY RATE 22/min or greater, SYSTOLIC BLOOD PRESSURE 100 mm Hg or less, and ALTERED MENTATION. She meets all three — respirations 26/min, systolic pressure 96 mm Hg, and a change from fully oriented to oriented to person only — so her score is 3. The common errors are adding points for the fever, the leukocytosis, the lactate, or the creatinine; none of those are qSOFA components, though all support the diagnosis. A score of 2 or more identifies a patient at high risk of poor outcome and should prompt full assessment. The framing that organizes this: sepsis is the HOST RESPONSE, not the organism — which is why cultures are negative in 30–50% of cases, why no single criterion has adequate sensitivity or specificity, and why five competing scores exist rather than one test. Infection plus organ dysfunction is sepsis; add profound circulatory AND cellular/metabolic derangement and it is septic shock, which is why lactate sits in the treatment bundle.

wrongExplanations.0: A score of 0 would require a respiratory rate below 22/min, a systolic pressure above 100 mm Hg, and normal mentation. All three of her values cross their thresholds.
wrongExplanations.1: A score of 1 counts only one criterion — typically the confusion, while overlooking that a respiratory rate of 26/min and a systolic pressure of 96 mm Hg each score as well.
wrongExplanations.2: A score of 2 is the most common wrong answer and usually comes from missing one threshold: either not counting 26/min as meeting the 22/min cutoff, or assuming hypotension requires a systolic pressure below 90 mm Hg. The qSOFA cutoff is 100 mm Hg or less, and hers is 96.

questions.eli5: There is a quick three-part bedside check for how sick an infected patient is: breathing fast, low blood pressure, and acting confused. She has all three, so she scores the maximum. Fever and abnormal blood tests are worrying but are not part of this particular score.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV infection is to begin antiretroviral therapy. His CD4 count is 210/μL and his plasma HIV RNA level is 84,000 copies/mL. The regimen selected consists of tenofovir, emtricitabine, and dolutegravir. Which of the following steps in the HIV replication cycle is inhibited by dolutegravir?
choices: A. Attachment of gp120 to the host CD4 receptor
B. Cleavage of the gag and pol precursor polyproteins
C. Fusion of the viral and host membranes mediated by gp41
D. Insertion of proviral DNA into the host cell genome
E. Synthesis of DNA from the viral RNA template
questions.explanation: Dolutegravir is an integrase strand transfer inhibitor. After reverse transcription produces double-stranded DNA, the viral enzyme INTEGRASE splices that DNA into the host genome, creating the provirus — the step that makes infection permanent. Blocking it leaves viral DNA unintegrated and unable to direct production of progeny. The three HIV structural genes anchor the rest of the map: ENV encodes the envelope glycoproteins gp120 (attachment to CD4) and gp41 (fusion); GAG encodes the core structural proteins; and POL encodes the enzymes — reverse transcriptase, integrase, and protease. Each of the other options is the target of a different drug class, and two of them are the targets of the other agents in this very regimen: tenofovir and emtricitabine are both reverse transcriptase inhibitors.

wrongExplanations.0: Attachment of gp120 to CD4 is blocked by the attachment inhibitor fostemsavir. It is the first step of entry and occurs outside the cell, long before integration.
wrongExplanations.1: Cleavage of the gag and pol precursor polyproteins is performed by the VIRAL protease during maturation of the budding particle, and is blocked by protease inhibitors such as darunavir. Resistance to this class is uncommon in patients not previously treated with one.
wrongExplanations.2: gp41-mediated fusion is blocked by enfuvirtide. Like attachment, it is an entry step and precedes any nucleic acid synthesis.
wrongExplanations.4: Synthesis of DNA from the viral RNA template is reverse transcription, blocked by both nucleoside and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors — including the tenofovir and emtricitabine he is already receiving. This is the strongest distractor precisely because it names a step his regimen genuinely targets, just not with dolutegravir. Note the class fact: a SINGLE point mutation can knock out the whole non-nucleoside class, because all its members bind the same allosteric pocket.

questions.eli5: HIV has to paste its own genetic code into the cell's DNA to take up permanent residence. One viral enzyme does that pasting, and this drug jams it. Other drugs in the same regimen block an earlier step, where the virus copies its RNA into DNA.

questions.stem:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the office by his parents because of a draining mass in the right axilla for 2 weeks. He has had three episodes of pneumonia, a liver abscess at 18 months of age, and recurrent skin abscesses. He is at the 5th percentile for weight. A maternal uncle died in childhood of an overwhelming infection. His temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F) and pulse is 118/min. Physical examination shows a 3-cm fluctuant right axillary mass with surrounding induration and scattered healed scars over the trunk. Tonsillar tissue is present and appears normal. Laboratory studies show:

    Leukocyte count                 16,800/mm3
      Segmented neutrophils         72%
    Serum IgG, IgA, and IgM         Within normal limits for age
    Absolute lymphocyte count       Within normal limits for age

Culture of drainage from the mass grows Serratia marcescens. A dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry assay shows an absent oxidative burst. Which of the following best explains this patient's susceptibility to this organism?
choices: A. Absent Bruton tyrosine kinase, so mature B cells are not produced
B. Absent NADPH oxidase activity, so catalase-positive organisms are not killed
C. Defective common gamma chain, so T-cell and B-cell development fails
D. Deficiency of adenosine deaminase, so lymphocyte precursors undergo apoptosis
E. Failure of leukocyte adhesion molecule expression, so neutrophils cannot leave the vasculature
questions.explanation: The absent oxidative burst on dihydrorhodamine testing is diagnostic of chronic granulomatous disease. Without NADPH oxidase the phagocyte cannot mount a respiratory burst, so it makes no hydrogen peroxide of its own. The elegant consequence is which organisms it can still handle: a CATALASE-NEGATIVE organism generates hydrogen peroxide and cannot destroy it, so the phagocyte simply BORROWS the bug's own peroxide and kills it. A CATALASE-POSITIVE organism destroys its own peroxide, leaving the phagocyte with nothing to work with — so it survives inside. Those are the organisms that define the disease: Staphylococcus aureus, Serratia marcescens, Aspergillus, Nocardia, and Burkholderia. The granuloma is the standoff, macrophages walling off organisms they cannot kill. This is a PHAGOCYTE disorder — about 10% of primary immunodeficiencies — which is why his neutrophil count and immunoglobulins are normal: the cells are present in normal numbers, they simply do not work. The maternal uncle fits X-linked inheritance.

wrongExplanations.0: Bruton agammaglobulinemia is an ANTIBODY deficiency (antibody defects are about 65% of primary immunodeficiencies). It presents after roughly 6 months, when maternal IgG wanes, with pyogenic infections by encapsulated organisms, and gives LOW immunoglobulins with ABSENT tonsils and atrophic nodes. His immunoglobulins are normal and his tonsils are present.
wrongExplanations.2: A common gamma chain defect is X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency, the most common form. Receptors for several interleukins share that chain, so both T- and B-cell arms fail, producing profound lymphopenia and opportunistic infection in early infancy. His absolute lymphocyte count is normal.
wrongExplanations.3: Adenosine deaminase deficiency is the autosomal recessive form of severe combined immunodeficiency: accumulated purines inhibit ribonucleotide reductase and rapidly dividing lymphocyte precursors die. It presents from about month 2 with Pneumocystis pneumonia and thrush, with a very low lymphocyte count — not with a normal count and a bacterial abscess at age 3.
wrongExplanations.4: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency prevents neutrophils from exiting vessels, so the classic findings are DELAYED separation of the umbilical cord, infections WITHOUT pus, and a very high circulating neutrophil count. This boy forms abscesses — pus that is full of neutrophils — so his cells are arriving; they simply cannot kill what they engulf.

Some bacteria helpfully make that chemical themselves and get killed with their own supply. The ones that destroy their own — like this one — survive inside the cell, so his body walls them off into lumps instead.
